subject: Biology
title: Human Health and Disease
summary: The chapter covers what health means, the common infectious diseases of humans (typhoid, pneumonia, common cold, malaria, amoebiasis, ascariasis, filariasis, ringworm) and how they spread, the two arms of immunity with the lymphoid organs behind them, AIDS, cancer, and drug and alcohol abuse. It is a fact-heavy, diagram-heavy chapter where the examiner rewards exact NCERT names, the Plasmodium life cycle, the antibody structure and the HIV replication cycle.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 12 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper. This chapter sits in Unit VIII, Biology and Human Welfare, which carries 12 marks in the CBSE blueprint shared with Microbes in Human Welfare. Human Health and Disease usually takes the larger share: expect a couple of 1-mark items, a 2-mark, a 3-mark and frequently a 5-mark or a case-based question drawn from malaria, immunity, AIDS or cancer.

question_types.note: Pathogen–disease–organ matching (Salmonella typhi, Wuchereria, Entamoeba, Rhinovirus), the vector of a disease, the Widal test, the cell that releases histamine, the stage of Plasmodium injected by the mosquito, the class of antibody in colostrum, the source plant of heroin or cocaine, the neurotransmitter cocaine interferes with.

Secondary response is stronger because of memory cells; colostrum gives passive immunity; malignant tumours metastasise; HIV is a retrovirus; breast-fed babies are better protected; fungal infections thrive in heat and moisture; Gambusia controls mosquito larvae.

Innate versus acquired immunity, active versus passive immunity, benign versus malignant tumour, primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, role of spleen or lymph nodes, why haemozoin causes chills, how breast feeding protects the infant, what a vaccine contains, role of mast cells in allergy, tolerance and withdrawal symptoms.

Four barriers of innate immunity, the antibody molecule with labels, how HIV destroys the immune system, why cancer cells differ from normal cells and how cancer is detected, the transmission of amoebiasis, ascariasis, malaria and pneumonia, the public health measures against vector-borne diseases, the harmful effects of drug abuse and how adolescents can be protected.

Life cycle of Plasmodium with the events in the two hosts and a labelled diagram; replication of HIV in the body and the events leading to AIDS; lymphoid organs and the structure and function of an antibody; cancer causes, detection and treatment; drug abuse (causes, addiction, dependence, effects, prevention).

A passage on a patient with recurrent fever and chills (malaria), a graph of primary and secondary immune response, an ELISA report and HIV transmission, or a scenario about a teenager and drug dependence, followed by four sub-questions.

Innate immunity: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers

Cancer: contact inhibition, benign versus malignant, metastasis, carcinogens, oncogenes, detection and treatment

sections.heading: 7.0 Introduction: what health is and what disease is
sections.body:
The chapter opens by fixing what the word health means, because students tend to write 'absence of disease' and lose the mark. NCERT defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Being free of disease is only a part of it; a person who is physically sound but under constant mental stress is not healthy in this sense.

There is a small piece of history that examiners occasionally pick out. The Greek physician Hippocrates and the Indian Ayurveda system held that health was a balance of four humours and that disease came from a disturbance of them. Two developments in the modern era ended that view: William Harvey's discovery of blood circulation using the experimental method, and the demonstration with a thermometer that a person supposedly carrying 'black bile' had a normal body temperature. Later, biology showed that health is affected by three groups of causes: genetic disorders (defects a child is born with), infections, and lifestyle (food, water, rest, exercise, habits).

Why does health matter beyond the individual? Good health raises productivity and brings economic prosperity, lengthens the life span and reduces infant and maternal mortality. NCERT lists the things that maintain health: a balanced diet, personal hygiene, regular exercise (yoga is named as one that has been practised since ancient times), awareness about diseases and their effects, vaccination against infectious diseases, proper disposal of wastes, control of vectors and hygienic food and water resources.

A disease is any condition in which the functioning of one or more organs or systems of the body is adversely affected, with characteristic signs and symptoms. Diseases are grouped into infectious ones, which spread from one person to another (they are still the major cause of death), and non-infectious ones, which do not spread; NCERT's example is cancer, the major cause of death among non-infectious diseases. Drug and alcohol abuse is treated separately because it damages health without any pathogen.

formulas.expr: Health = complete physical, mental and social well-being
Causes affecting health: genetic disorders, infections, lifestyle

sections.tip: If asked to 'define health', write the full NCERT phrase. 'Absence of disease' on its own is marked wrong.

sections.heading: 7.1 Common Diseases in Humans: bacterial and viral diseases (typhoid, pneumonia, common cold)
sections.body:
Organisms that cause disease are pathogens. NCERT covers them by group: bacteria, viruses, protozoans, helminths and fungi. Most pathogens enter with food and water, multiply, and interfere with the normal function of an organ. For each disease you need four things ready: the pathogen (with correct spelling and italics for the genus and species), the organ or tissue attacked, the symptoms, and the mode of transmission. One-mark questions come from any of the four.

Typhoid. Caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi. It enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and then migrates through blood to other organs. Symptoms are sustained high fever (39° to 40°C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite. In severe cases intestinal perforation can lead to death. It is confirmed by the Widal test. NCERT tells the story of Mary Mallon, 'Typhoid Mary', a cook who was a carrier and spread typhoid for years through the food she prepared; carriers matter because they show no symptoms.

Pneumonia. Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, which infect the alveoli of the lungs. The alveoli fill with fluid, so gas exchange is severely reduced. Symptoms: fever, chills, cough and headache; in severe cases the lips and fingernails turn grey to bluish because of poor oxygenation. It spreads by inhaling droplets or aerosols released by an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils.

Common cold. Caused by rhinoviruses, which infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs; this 'not the lungs' phrase is a favourite fill-in-the-blank. Symptoms: nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness, lasting 3 to 7 days. It spreads through droplets from coughs and sneezes and through contaminated objects such as pens, books, cups, doorknobs and computer keyboards.

Keep the bacterial and viral diseases separate in your head: a question like 'name a bacterial disease of the respiratory tract' wants pneumonia, while 'a viral disease of the respiratory tract' wants common cold.

formulas.expr: Typhoid: Salmonella typhi → small intestine → Widal test
Pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae → alveoli
where: lips and fingernails grey to bluish

formulas.expr: Common cold: rhinoviruses → nose and respiratory passage, not lungs

sections.tip: Write genus and species in italics and spell them exactly: Salmonella typhi, not 'Salmonella typhii'. A wrong pathogen name costs the whole mark in a 1-mark question.

sections.heading: 7.1 Common Diseases in Humans: malaria and the life cycle of Plasmodium
sections.body:
Malaria is the single most examined disease in the chapter, because it carries a life cycle with two hosts and a diagram (NCERT Figure 7.1). It is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium. Three species are named: P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum; P. falciparum causes the most serious, malignant malaria, which can be fatal. The vector is the female Anopheles mosquito; only the female bites because she needs a blood meal.

In the human host. When an infected female Anopheles bites, Plasmodium enters the blood as sporozoites, the infective stage. Sporozoites reach the liver and multiply in the liver cells. The parasites then burst out and attack the red blood cells (RBCs), where they multiply further and rupture the RBCs. The rupture releases a toxic substance, haemozoin, and it is haemozoin that produces the characteristic chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. Some parasites in the RBCs develop into the sexual stages, male and female gametocytes. A question on 'why does a malaria patient get fever in cycles' is answered with the RBC rupture and haemozoin.

In the mosquito. When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, she takes up gametocytes with the blood. Fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's gut, forming sporozoites which are stored in the salivary glands. When this mosquito bites another human, the sporozoites are injected and the cycle begins again.

So the parasite needs two hosts: the human, in which the asexual stages occur, and the female Anopheles, in which the sexual stages (fertilisation and sporozoite formation) occur. Because the mosquito is where sexual reproduction takes place, it is called the definitive host and the human the intermediate host, though NCERT itself only says 'two hosts'.

For the 5-mark version, write the human phase and the mosquito phase as separate paragraphs, draw the cycle with the mosquito at the top and the human at the bottom, and label sporozoites, liver cells, RBCs, haemozoin release, gametocytes, fertilisation in the gut and sporozoites in the salivary glands.

formulas.expr: Sporozoite (infective stage) → liver → RBCs → rupture + haemozoin → chill and fever every 3–4 days
where: toxic substance released on RBC rupture

formulas.expr: Gametocytes → mosquito gut (fertilisation) → sporozoites in salivary glands

sections.tip: The stage injected by the mosquito is the sporozoite; the stage the mosquito picks up is the gametocyte. Students swap these under pressure.

sections.heading: 7.1 Common Diseases in Humans: amoebiasis, ascariasis, filariasis and ringworm
sections.body:
Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery). Caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, a parasite of the large intestine. Symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, and stools with excess mucous and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers, transferring the parasite from the faeces of an infected person to food and food products; drinking water and food contaminated by faecal matter are the main sources. 'Mechanical carrier' is the precise phrase to use; the fly does not host the parasite the way Anopheles hosts Plasmodium.

Ascariasis. Caused by the common roundworm Ascaris, an intestinal parasite (a helminth). Symptoms: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage. Eggs of the parasite are excreted with faeces and contaminate soil, water and plants; a healthy person gets infected through contaminated vegetables, fruits and water. So it is a soil- and water-borne infection acquired by ingestion, not by a vector.

Filariasis (elephantiasis). Caused by the filarial worms Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi. They live in the lymphatic vessels (usually of the lower limbs) and cause slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs in which they live for many years. The gross deformity of the limbs and of the genital organs is what gives the name elephantiasis. The pathogen is transmitted by the bite of female mosquito vectors (the Culex mosquito, though NCERT just says female mosquito).

Ringworm. A fungal infection caused by the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Symptoms: dry, scaly lesions on the skin, nails and scalp with intense itching. Heat and moisture help the fungi grow, which is why the infection is common in skin folds such as the groin and between the toes. It is acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or combs of infected people.

Examiners like a table with four columns: disease, pathogen, organ affected, mode of transmission. Practise writing all eight diseases of section 7.1 in that format; it is the fastest way to secure a 3-mark 'complete the table' question.

formulas.expr: Amoebiasis: Entamoeba histolytica → large intestine; housefly = mechanical carrier
Ascariasis: Ascaris → intestine; eggs in faeces → soil, water, plants
where: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, intestinal blockage

formulas.expr: Filariasis: Wuchereria bancrofti, W. malayi → lymphatic vessels of lower limbs
Ringworm: Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton → skin, nails, scalp

sections.tip: Filariasis is the only helminth disease in the chapter with a vector; ascariasis spreads by contaminated food and water, not by a mosquito.

sections.heading: 7.1 Prevention and control of infectious diseases
sections.body:
Since many of these diseases are preventable, the chapter ends section 7.1 with a set of public health measures. This paragraph is the source of the frequently asked 'suggest public health measures against infectious diseases' and 'how would you control vector-borne diseases' questions, and the exercise question 7.1 is the same thing.

Personal hygiene means keeping the body clean, and consuming clean drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits. Public hygiene means proper disposal of waste and excreta, periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks, and observing standard practices of hygiene in public catering. These measures are aimed at the diseases that spread through food and water, such as typhoid, amoebiasis and ascariasis.

For air-borne diseases such as pneumonia and common cold, the advice is to avoid close contact with the infected person or their belongings, in addition to the measures above.

For vector-borne diseases such as malaria and filariasis, the most important step is to control or eliminate the vectors and their breeding places. NCERT's list: avoid stagnation of water in and around residential areas; regularly clean household coolers; use mosquito nets; introduce fish like Gambusia in ponds, which feed on mosquito larvae; spray insecticides in ditches, drainage areas and swamps; and fit doors and windows with wire mesh to keep mosquitoes out. The chapter notes that these steps have become especially important given the recent widespread incidence of dengue and chikungunya in many parts of India, both spread by the Aedes mosquito.

Finally, the discovery of vaccines and immunisation programmes has allowed the eradication of smallpox and the control of polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus; and biotechnology is producing safer vaccines. Antibiotics and other drugs have made it possible to treat infectious diseases effectively. This is the answer to exercise 7.2, 'how has the study of biology helped us control infectious diseases'.

formulas.expr: Vector control: no stagnant water, clean coolers, mosquito nets, Gambusia in ponds, insecticide in ditches and swamps, wire mesh
Aedes mosquito → dengue, chikungunya

sections.tip: When asked for measures, sort them under personal hygiene, public hygiene, air-borne and vector-borne; a structured answer picks up all the marking points.

sections.heading: 7.2 Immunity and 7.2.1 Innate Immunity
sections.body:
Immunity is the overall ability of the host to fight the disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system. Every day we are exposed to a large number of infectious agents, yet only a few of these exposures result in disease, because of this ability. Immunity is of two types: innate and acquired.

Innate immunity is non-specific and is present at birth. It provides different types of barriers to the entry of foreign agents into the body. NCERT lists four barriers, and a 3-mark question asks for all four with examples.

Physical barriers. The skin is the main barrier and prevents the entry of micro-organisms. The mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts helps in trapping microbes.

Physiological barriers. Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes prevent microbial growth. These work by chemical conditions rather than by physically blocking entry.

Cellular barriers. Certain types of leukocytes (white blood cells), namely the polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils) and monocytes, and the natural killer (NK) lymphocytes in the blood, as well as macrophages in tissues, can phagocytose and destroy microbes. The question 'name the cellular barrier' is answered with these cells; 'monocytes' and 'natural killer cells' are the two most asked names.

Cytokine barriers. Virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection. Note that interferons are secreted by infected cells and act on neighbouring healthy cells; a common error is to say they destroy the virus directly.

Write each barrier with its two or three examples. A common lost mark is to list the skin under physiological barriers or the stomach acid under physical barriers.

formulas.expr: Innate immunity = non-specific, present at birth, four barriers

sections.tip: Interferons are produced by virus-infected cells to protect non-infected cells. Write both halves of that sentence.

sections.heading: 7.2.2 Acquired Immunity: B cells, T cells and the antibody molecule
sections.body:
Acquired immunity is pathogen specific and is characterised by memory. When the body meets a pathogen for the first time it produces a response called the primary response, which is of low intensity. A subsequent encounter with the same pathogen produces a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response. The reason is the memory of the first encounter, carried in memory cells. This primary-versus-secondary contrast is asked as a 2-mark question and also as a graph in case-based questions: the secondary curve rises faster, higher and lasts longer.

Acquired immunity is carried out by two special types of lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes. The B-lymphocytes produce an army of proteins called antibodies in response to pathogens in the blood. The T-cells do not secrete antibodies themselves but help B cells produce them.

Structure of an antibody (NCERT Figure 7.2). Each antibody molecule has four peptide chains: two small light chains and two longer heavy chains, so an antibody is written H2L2. The chains form a Y shape; the tips of the arms carry the antigen-binding sites. The chains are held by disulphide bonds. Different types of antibodies are produced in the body: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG (the other class, IgD, is not named in NCERT).

Humoral immune response. Because antibodies are found in the blood, the response mediated by antibodies is called the humoral immune response, or antibody-mediated response; 'humor' is an old word for body fluid.

Cell-mediated immunity (CMI). The T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity. Its importance shows up in organ transplantation. When a patient receives a graft of kidney, heart, eye or liver from a donor, the body is able to distinguish 'self' from 'nonself', and the cell-mediated immune response is responsible for graft rejection. That is why tissue (blood group) matching is done before grafting and why patients are given immuno-suppressants for life afterwards. 'Which type of immune response causes graft rejection?' is a standard 1-mark question and the answer is cell-mediated immunity.

So the two acquired responses are: B cells and antibodies (humoral) against pathogens in body fluids, and T cells (cell-mediated) against infected or foreign cells. Both keep memory cells.

formulas.expr: Antibody = H<sub>2</sub>L<sub>2</sub> (2 heavy + 2 light peptide chains, Y-shaped)
where: tip of each arm of the Y

formulas.expr: Primary response (low) → memory → secondary / anamnestic response (high)
Graft rejection = cell-mediated immunity (T cells)

sections.tip: In the antibody diagram, label the antigen-binding site, heavy chain, light chain and the disulphide bonds; those four labels are what the marking scheme looks for.

sections.heading: 7.2.3 Active and Passive Immunity
sections.body:
This short section gives the chapter's most repeated 2-mark differentiation. Learn it as two clean definitions with an example of each.

Active immunity. When a host is exposed to antigens, which may be living or dead microbes or other proteins, the host's own body produces antibodies. This is active immunity. It is slow and takes time to give its full effective response, but it is long-lasting because memory cells are formed. It can be induced in two ways: by natural infection, or deliberately by injecting microbes during immunisation. Both count as active immunity because in both the body makes its own antibodies.

Passive immunity. When ready-made antibodies are given directly to protect the body against foreign agents, it is passive immunity. It is immediate in effect but short-lived, because no memory cells are formed and the borrowed antibodies are eventually broken down. NCERT gives two natural examples: the yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant; and the foetus receives some antibodies from its mother through the placenta during pregnancy. Deliberate passive immunity, such as anti-tetanus serum, is covered in the next section.

The colostrum point is the basis of the popular question 'why are breast-fed babies more immune to diseases than bottle-fed babies?'. The answer is that mother's milk, especially colostrum, contains IgA antibodies that bottle-fed babies do not receive, so the breast-fed baby has passive immunity in its first weeks. Name the antibody class, IgA; that is where the second mark sits.

A quick way to fix the difference: 'active' means the body is active in making antibodies; 'passive' means the body passively receives antibodies made elsewhere.

formulas.expr: Active: own antibodies, slow, long-lasting (infection or vaccine)
Passive: ready-made antibodies, immediate, short-lived (colostrum IgA, placenta, antitoxin)

sections.tip: Vaccination is active immunity, even though something is injected. Injecting an antitoxin or antibodies is passive.

sections.heading: 7.2.4 Vaccination and Immunisation
sections.body:
The principle of immunisation or vaccination is based on the property of memory of the immune system. In vaccination, a preparation of antigenic proteins of the pathogen, or inactivated/weakened pathogen (a vaccine), is introduced into the body. The antibodies produced in the body against these antigens neutralise the pathogenic agents during actual infection. The vaccines also generate memory B and T cells, which recognise the pathogen quickly on subsequent exposure and overwhelm the invaders with a massive production of antibodies. Vaccination is therefore an example of artificially induced active immunity.

NCERT then describes passive immunisation. If a person is infected with some deadly microbes to which a quick immune response is required, as in tetanus, we need to inject preformed antibodies, or antitoxin (a preparation containing antibodies to the toxin) directly. Even in cases of snake bites, the injection given to patients contains preformed antibodies against the snake venom. This type of immunisation is called passive immunisation. The examiner's question is usually 'why is anti-tetanus serum given to a person with a deep wound instead of a vaccine?', and the answer is that the vaccine would take days to produce antibodies while the toxin acts fast, so ready-made antibodies are given for immediate protection.

The last paragraph is about modern vaccine production. Recombinant DNA technology allows the production of antigenic polypeptides of a pathogen in bacteria or yeast; vaccines produced this way allow large-scale production and hence greater availability for immunisation. NCERT's example is the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast. This links to Chapter 10 (Biotechnology and its Applications), and 'name the organism used to produce hepatitis B vaccine' is a standard 1-mark item: yeast.

NCERT exercise 7.5 asks you to discuss what 'a suitable gene' means in the context of DNA vaccines. The expected sense: a suitable gene is the piece of pathogen DNA that codes for an antigenic protein of the pathogen; when introduced into the host it is expressed to produce that antigen, which triggers antibody production and memory without any live pathogen.

formulas.expr: Vaccine = antigenic proteins of pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen → antibodies + memory B and T cells
Antitoxin / preformed antibodies (tetanus, snake bite) = passive immunisation
Hepatitis B vaccine produced in yeast by recombinant DNA technology

sections.tip: Tetanus and snake bite are the two NCERT examples of passive immunisation. Quote at least one.

sections.heading: 7.2.5 Allergies
sections.body:
Most of us know someone who starts sneezing when the dust flies. That is an allergy. NCERT defines allergy as the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment. The substances to which such an immune response is produced are called allergens. Examples of allergens: mites in dust, pollens, animal dander.

The mechanism is what earns marks. The antibodies produced against allergens are of the IgE type. Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells. So the chain is: allergen enters → IgE antibodies are made → on subsequent exposure the allergen binds IgE on mast cells → mast cells release histamine and serotonin → inflammatory symptoms. The symptoms NCERT lists: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing.

To determine the cause of an allergy, the patient is exposed to or injected with very small doses of possible allergens and the reactions studied. Treatment uses drugs like anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids, which quickly reduce the symptoms. The question 'what is the role of mast cells in allergy?' wants 'release of histamine and serotonin'; the question 'name the antibody involved in allergy' wants IgE; and 'name two drugs that reduce allergic symptoms' wants any two of the three listed.

The section ends with a social observation that examiners turn into a reasoning question: modern-day lifestyle has resulted in lowering of immunity and more sensitivity to allergens. More and more children in metro cities of India suffer from allergies and asthma due to sensitivity to the environment, and this may be because of the protected environment provided early in life. If asked why children in cities are more allergic, this is the expected answer.

formulas.expr: Allergen → IgE → mast cells release histamine and serotonin → sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, breathing difficulty

sections.tip: Two chemicals, histamine and serotonin; one antibody class, IgE; one cell, the mast cell. Do not write IgG for allergy.

sections.heading: 7.2.6 Auto Immunity
sections.body:
This is the shortest section in the chapter, but it turns up as a 1- or 2-mark question because the definition is precise. Memory-based acquired immunity evolved in higher vertebrates on the basis of the ability to differentiate foreign organisms (for example pathogens) from self-cells. Although we still do not fully understand the basis of this, two corollaries of this ability have to be understood.

The first is that higher vertebrates can distinguish foreign molecules and foreign organisms from their own; this is the basis of graft rejection, which section 7.2.2 explained. The second is the failure case: sometimes, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body attacks self-cells. This results in damage to the body and is called an auto-immune disease. NCERT's single named example is rheumatoid arthritis, which affects many people in our society. If a question asks for another example you may add ones from general knowledge such as type 1 diabetes or myasthenia gravis, but rheumatoid arthritis is the safe NCERT answer.

Write the definition in two sentences: the immune system normally distinguishes self from non-self; in an auto-immune disease this discrimination fails and the immune system attacks the body's own cells. Then give the example. Students sometimes confuse auto-immunity with allergy: allergy is an exaggerated response to a harmless external antigen, auto-immunity is a response against the body's own cells. Another confusion is with immunodeficiency (AIDS), where the immune system is too weak; in auto-immunity it is misdirected, not weak. Keeping these three apart is enough to answer any variant of the question.

formulas.expr: Auto-immune disease = immune system attacks self-cells (self/non-self discrimination fails)

sections.tip: Allergy is an over-reaction to a foreign antigen; auto-immunity is a reaction against self. Name rheumatoid arthritis.

sections.heading: 7.2.7 Immune System in the Body: lymphoid organs
sections.body:
The human immune system consists of lymphoid organs, tissues, cells and soluble molecules like antibodies. The system recognises foreign antigens, responds to them and remembers them. It also plays a role in allergic reactions, auto-immune diseases and organ transplantation. Lymphoid organs are the organs where the origin and/or maturation and proliferation of lymphocytes occur. They are of two kinds.

Primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and the thymus, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes. The bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells including lymphocytes are produced. The thymus is a lobed organ located near the heart and beneath the breastbone; it is quite large at the time of birth but keeps reducing in size with age and is very small by the time of puberty. Both bone marrow and thymus provide micro-environments for the development and maturation of T-lymphocytes (thymus) and B-lymphocytes (bone marrow). 'Why does the thymus shrink with age' and 'what would happen if the thymus were removed at birth' are the reasoning questions from here: without a thymus, T cells cannot mature, so cell-mediated immunity and the helper function for B cells are lost.

Secondary lymphoid organs are where the mature lymphocytes migrate after maturation and where they interact with the antigen and proliferate to become effector cells. They are the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and appendix.

Spleen. A large bean-shaped organ. It mainly contains lymphocytes and phagocytes. It acts as a filter of the blood by trapping blood-borne micro-organisms, and it has a large reservoir of erythrocytes. Those two roles are the 2-mark question on the spleen.

Lymph nodes. Small solid structures located at different points along the lymphatic system. They trap micro-organisms or other antigens that enter the lymph and tissue fluid. Antigens trapped in the lymph nodes activate the lymphocytes present there and cause the immune response.

MALT. Within the lining of the major tracts (respiratory, digestive and urogenital) there is lymphoid tissue called mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). It constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body. Exercise 7.7 asks for the full forms of MALT, CMI, AIDS, NACO and HIV; have all five ready.

formulas.expr: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (B cells mature) and thymus (T cells mature)
where: large at birth, reduces with age

formulas.expr: Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix
MALT ≈ 50% of lymphoid tissue
where: lining of respiratory, digestive, urogenital tracts

sections.tip: Bone marrow is both the origin of all blood cells and the site of B cell maturation; the thymus matures T cells. Label both as primary.

sections.heading: 7.3 AIDS
sections.body:
AIDS stands for Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome, a deficiency of the immune system acquired during the lifetime of an individual, indicating that it is not a congenital disease. 'Syndrome' means a group of symptoms. It was first reported in 1981 and in the following twenty-five years spread all over the world, killing more than 25 million persons (the NCERT figure).

AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), a member of a group of viruses called retroviruses, which have an envelope enclosing the RNA genome. Transmission generally occurs by (a) sexual contact with an infected person, (b) transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products, (c) sharing infected needles, as in the case of intravenous drug abusers, and (d) from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. So the people at high risk are those with multiple sexual partners, drug addicts who take drugs intravenously, individuals who require repeated blood transfusions, and children born to an HIV-infected mother. NCERT stresses that HIV does not spread by mere touch or physical contact; it spreads only through body fluids. There is always a time-lag between the infection and the appearance of AIDS symptoms, which can vary from a few months to 5 to 10 years.

Replication of HIV (NCERT Figure 7.3). After getting into the body, the virus enters macrophages. Its RNA genome replicates to form viral DNA with the help of the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cells to produce virus particles. The macrophages continue to produce virus and in this way act like an HIV factory. Simultaneously HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses. The progeny viruses released in the blood attack other helper T-lymphocytes. This is repeated, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body of the infected person. During this period the person suffers from bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss. Because of the loss of helper T cells the person becomes unable to produce any immune response, and is infected by bacteria, especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma. Note the order: macrophages first (the factory), then helper T cells (the count that falls).

Diagnosis is by ELISA (enzyme-linked immuno-sorbent assay). Treatment with anti-retroviral drugs is only partially effective; it can prolong life but cannot prevent death, which is inevitable.

Prevention. Since AIDS has no cure, prevention is the best option. In India, NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) and NGOs educate people. WHO has started programmes: making blood from blood banks safe from HIV, ensuring use of disposable needles and syringes in public and private hospitals, free distribution of condoms, controlling drug abuse, advocating safe sex and promoting regular check-ups for HIV in susceptible populations. Infection is regarded as a social problem, and infected people need help and sympathy rather than being shunned. 1 December is World AIDS Day.

formulas.expr: HIV RNA → (reverse transcriptase) → viral DNA → integrates into host DNA → new virus particles
Transmission: sexual contact, contaminated blood, shared needles, mother to child via placenta
Diagnosis ELISA · treatment anti-retroviral drugs · incubation 5–10 years · NACO · 1 December

sections.tip: HIV is diagnosed by ELISA, not by the Widal test (typhoid) or by biopsy (cancer). Do not mix the diagnostic tests.

sections.heading: 7.4 Cancer
sections.body:
Cancer is one of the most dreaded diseases and a major cause of death worldwide. The chapter explains what goes wrong in a cancer cell, what causes it, how it is detected and how it is treated; any of these can be a 3- or 5-mark question.

What a cancer cell is. Normal cells show a property called contact inhibition: contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells appear to have lost this property, so they continue to divide, giving rise to masses of cells called tumours. Tumours are of two types. Benign tumours normally remain confined to their original location, do not spread to other parts of the body and cause little damage. Malignant tumours are a mass of proliferating cells called neoplastic or tumour cells; they grow very rapidly, invade and damage the surrounding normal tissues, and compete with normal cells for vital nutrients. Cells sloughed from such tumours reach distant sites through blood, and wherever they get lodged they start a new tumour. This property is called metastasis, and it is the most feared property of malignant tumours. Exercise 7.12 (cancer cell versus normal cell) and 7.13 (metastasis) come straight from these lines.

Causes. The transformation of normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells may be induced by physical, chemical or biological agents called carcinogens. Ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionising radiations like UV cause DNA damage leading to neoplastic transformation. The chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke are the major cause of lung cancer. Cancer-causing viruses, called oncogenic viruses, have genes called viral oncogenes. Several genes called cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes have been identified in normal cells which, when activated under certain conditions, lead to the oncogenic transformation of the cells.

Detection and diagnosis. Early detection is essential. Cancer detection is based on biopsy and histopathological studies of the tissue, and blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in the case of leukaemias. In biopsy a piece of the suspected tissue cut into thin sections is stained and examined under the microscope by a pathologist. Techniques like radiography (use of X-rays), CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are very useful to detect cancers of the internal organs. CT uses X-rays to generate a three-dimensional image of the internals of an object; MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue. Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used for detection of certain cancers, and techniques of molecular biology can detect genes in individuals with inherited susceptibility to certain cancers.

Treatment. The common approaches are surgery, radiation therapy and immunotherapy. In radiotherapy tumour cells are irradiated lethally while taking care of the surrounding normal tissues. Several chemotherapeutic drugs are used, and most have side effects such as hair loss and anaemia. Most cancers are treated by a combination of surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Because tumour cells avoid detection and destruction by the immune system, patients are given substances called biological response modifiers such as α-interferon, which activate their immune system and help destroy the tumour; this is immunotherapy.

formulas.expr: Normal cells: contact inhibition; cancer cells: lost it → tumour
Carcinogens: ionising (X-rays, γ-rays), non-ionising (UV), chemical (tobacco smoke), biological (oncogenic viruses with viral oncogenes)
where: normal-cell genes that can be activated to cause cancer

formulas.expr: Detection: biopsy + histopathology, blood and bone marrow tests, radiography, CT, MRI, antibodies against cancer-specific antigens

sections.tip: Metastasis is the property of malignant tumours, never benign ones. Define it with the words 'sloughed off', 'blood' and 'new tumour at a distant site'.

sections.heading: 7.5 Drugs and Alcohol Abuse; 7.5.1 Adolescence; 7.5.2 Addiction and Dependence
sections.body:
NCERT reports that surveys and statistics show a rise in the use of drugs and alcohol, especially among the youth, and treats the topic as a health issue. The drugs commonly abused are opioids, cannabinoids and coca alkaloids, all obtained from flowering plants, plus some from fungi.

Opioids are drugs that bind to specific opioid receptors present in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin, commonly called smack, is chemically diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions. Morphine itself is a very effective sedative and painkiller and is useful in patients who have undergone surgery.

Cannabinoids are a group of chemicals that interact with cannabinoid receptors present principally in the brain. Natural cannabinoids are obtained from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa. The flower tops, leaves and resin are used in various combinations to produce marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja. Cannabinoids affect the cardiovascular system, and these days they are also being abused by some sportspersons.

Coca alkaloid or cocaine is obtained from the coca plant Erythroxylum coca, native to South America. It interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine. Cocaine, commonly called coke or crack, is usually snorted. It has a potent stimulating action on the central nervous system, producing a sense of euphoria and increased energy; excessive dosage causes hallucinations. Other plants with hallucinogenic properties are Atropa belladona and Datura. Drugs used as medicines to help patients cope with mental illnesses like depression and insomnia, such as barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and LSD, are also often abused. Smoking, alcohol and drugs are all forms of abuse.

7.5.1 Adolescence. Adolescence is the period between 12 and 18 years, a bridge between childhood and adulthood, marked by biological and behavioural changes. It is a vulnerable phase. NCERT names the causes of first use: curiosity, need for adventure and excitement, and experimentation; the pressure of peers; the wish to excel in school or examinations; unstable or unsupportive family structures; and television, movies, newspapers and the internet that promote the perception that smoking or drinking is 'cool'.

7.5.2 Addiction and dependence. Addiction is a psychological attachment to certain effects such as euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being, which drives people to take the drug even when it is not needed. With repeated use, the tolerance level of the receptors in the body increases, so the receptors respond only to higher doses, and this is what leads to greater intake and addiction. Dependence is the tendency of the body to show a characteristic and unpleasant withdrawal syndrome if regular intake is abruptly discontinued; the symptoms include anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating, and in severe cases they may be life-threatening. Dependence leads the patient to ignore social norms in order to get sufficient funds to satisfy the need.

formulas.expr: Heroin (smack) = diacetylmorphine, from Papaver somniferum latex; opioid receptors in CNS and GI tract; depressant
Cannabinoids from Cannabis sativa inflorescences (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja); receptors in brain; cardiovascular effects
Cocaine (coke/crack) from Erythroxylum coca; interferes with dopamine transport; CNS stimulant; hallucinations in excess
Addiction = psychological attachment; tolerance rises; dependence = withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating)

sections.tip: Heroin is a depressant; cocaine is a stimulant. The two are asked as a contrast, and students often reverse them.

sections.heading: 7.5.3 Effects of Drug/Alcohol Abuse and 7.5.4 Prevention and Control
sections.body:
Effects. The immediate adverse effects of drugs and alcohol are reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence. Excessive doses lead to coma and death due to respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage. A combination of drugs, or their intake with alcohol, generally results in overdosing and even death. The warning signs among youth include drop in academic performance, unexplained absence from school or college, lack of interest in personal hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, fatigue, aggressive and rebellious behaviour, deteriorating relationships with family and friends, loss of interest in hobbies, change in sleeping and eating habits, fluctuations in weight and appetite. There can be far-reaching implications too. If an abuser cannot get money, he or she may turn to stealing. Drug and alcohol abuse also affects the family and society, and intravenous drug abusers who share needles are at risk of serious infections like AIDS and hepatitis B. The viruses in both cases are transferred through infected needles and syringes; AIDS is fatal, and hepatitis B damages the liver. Chronic use of drugs and alcohol damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis). Use during pregnancy adversely affects the foetus.

Drugs in sports. Some sportspersons misuse cannabinoids, narcotic analgesics, anabolic steroids, diuretics and certain hormones to increase muscle strength and bulk and to promote aggressiveness. Anabolic steroids have side effects that are asked as a 3-mark question. In females: masculinisation (features like males), increased aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles, excessive hair growth on face and body, enlargement of clitoris, deepening of voice. In males: acne, increased aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, reduction of the size of the testicles, decreased sperm production, potential for kidney and liver dysfunction, breast enlargement, premature baldness, enlargement of the prostate gland. In the young, in both boys and girls, severe facial and body acne and premature closure of the growth centres of the long bones, resulting in stunted growth.

Prevention and control. Prevention is better than cure, and the age most at risk is adolescence. NCERT's measures: (i) avoid undue peer pressure, respecting each child's own choice and personality rather than pushing to perform beyond their threshold in studies, sports or other activities; (ii) education and counselling to face problems and stresses and to accept disappointments and failures as a part of life, channelising the child's energy into sports, reading, music and yoga; (iii) seeking help from parents and peers so that guidance is received immediately; (iv) looking for danger signs, so that alert parents and teachers can take the proper steps; and (v) seeking professional and medical help from psychologists and psychiatrists and from de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes, with which the affected individual can overcome the problem completely and lead a normal life.

Tobacco, alcohol and nicotine belong here too. Nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline, which raise blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking is associated with cancers of the lung, urinary bladder, throat and oral cavity, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease and gastric ulcer; it increases carbon monoxide in the blood and reduces the oxygen concentration, causing oxygen deficiency in the body.

formulas.expr: Overdose → coma, death by respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage
Anabolic steroids in the young → premature closure of growth centres of long bones → stunted growth
Nicotine → adrenal gland → adrenaline + nor-adrenaline → ↑ blood pressure, ↑ heart rate; CO ↑, O<sub>2</sub> ↓
Prevention: avoid peer pressure, education and counselling, help from parents and peers, watch danger signs, professional and medical help

sections.tip: For 'harmful effects of drug abuse' give at least four distinct points: behaviour, overdose death, infections from needles, organ damage, and sports side effects.

diagrams.title: Life cycle of Plasmodium (NCERT Fig 7.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a loop with a female Anopheles at the top and a human at the bottom. From the mosquito's bite show sporozoites entering blood, reaching liver cells and multiplying (label 'sporozoites enter liver', 'parasites reproduce asexually in liver cells'). Show parasites entering red blood cells, multiplying and rupturing them with the label 'release of haemozoin: chills and fever'. Show some parasites becoming male and female gametocytes in RBCs. Draw a second mosquito taking up gametocytes; in the mosquito show 'fertilisation and development in the gut' and 'sporozoites migrate to salivary glands'. Label the two hosts and mark the sexual stages in the mosquito, asexual in the human.

diagrams.title: Structure of an antibody molecule (NCERT Fig 7.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a Y-shaped molecule of four chains: two long heavy chains running from the base of the Y up into the arms, and two short light chains lying along the outside of each arm. Join the chains with short lines labelled disulphide bonds. Mark the tips of both arms as antigen-binding sites. Label heavy chain, light chain, antigen-binding site and disulphide bond, and write H2L2 beside it. Optionally mark the variable region at the tips and the constant region towards the stem.

diagrams.title: Replication of retrovirus / HIV in the host (NCERT Fig 7.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the HIV particle as an envelope enclosing RNA and label it. Show it entering a host cell (macrophage or helper T cell). Inside, draw the viral RNA being copied into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase (label the enzyme and 'viral DNA is produced by reverse transcriptase'). Show viral DNA entering the nucleus and being incorporated into the host cell DNA (label 'viral DNA incorporated into host genome'). Show the host DNA directing the formation of viral RNA and viral proteins, assembly of new viruses, and their release from the cell ('new viruses are produced'). Mark the direction with arrows in a single loop.

diagrams.title: Lymphoid organs in the human body
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an outline of the human body and mark: tonsils in the throat, thymus below the breastbone near the heart, spleen on the left below the diaphragm, lymph nodes in the neck, armpits and groin, Peyer's patches in the small intestine, appendix at the start of the large intestine, and bone marrow inside a long bone. Colour-code or label bone marrow and thymus as primary lymphoid organs and the rest as secondary lymphoid organs.

diagrams.title: Primary and secondary immune response (graph)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes: antibody concentration on the y-axis, time in days on the x-axis. Mark the first exposure to antigen; draw a small, slow curve that rises after a lag of several days, peaks low and falls (label 'primary response, IgM then IgG'). Mark the second exposure to the same antigen further along; draw a steep, tall curve that rises within a day or two, peaks much higher and stays up longer (label 'secondary or anamnestic response, mainly IgG, due to memory cells'). Write in a corner that the second curve is faster, larger and longer-lasting.

diagrams.title: Mechanism of an allergic reaction
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an allergen (pollen or dust mite) entering the body, B cells producing IgE antibodies, and the IgE attaching to the surface of a mast cell. On a second exposure show the allergen bridging two IgE molecules on the mast cell, and the mast cell degranulating with arrows labelled histamine and serotonin. Beside it list the effects: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, difficulty in breathing, and the drugs that block them: anti-histamine, adrenalin, steroids.

diagrams.title: Benign versus malignant tumour and metastasis
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two boxes of tissue. In the first, a compact ball of tumour cells enclosed within a boundary, not spreading, labelled 'benign tumour: confined, little damage'. In the second, a mass of neoplastic cells with irregular edges invading the neighbouring normal tissue, a few cells breaking off into a blood vessel, travelling and forming a new tumour in a distant organ. Label 'malignant tumour', 'invasion of surrounding tissue', 'cells sloughed into blood' and 'metastasis: new tumour at a distant site'. Add a note that normal cells show contact inhibition and cancer cells have lost it.

diagrams.title: Types of immunity (flow chart)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Start with a box 'Immunity' branching into 'Innate (non-specific, present at birth)' and 'Acquired (specific, with memory)'. Under innate, four boxes: physical (skin, mucus), physiological (stomach acid, saliva, tears), cellular (PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, NK cells, macrophages), cytokine (interferons). Under acquired, branch into 'Humoral: B cells, antibodies' and 'Cell-mediated: T cells'. Then a second split of acquired into 'Active (own antibodies: infection, vaccination; slow, long-lasting)' and 'Passive (ready-made antibodies: colostrum, placenta, antitoxin; immediate, short-lived)'.

ncert_questions.q: What are the various public health measures which you would suggest as safeguard against infectious diseases?
ncert_questions.a:
Public health measures against infectious diseases:

  • Personal hygiene: keeping the body clean; consuming clean drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits.
  • Public hygiene: proper disposal of waste and excreta; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks; standard practices of hygiene in public catering. These control food- and water-borne diseases such as typhoid, amoebiasis and ascariasis.
  • Air-borne diseases (pneumonia, common cold): avoid close contact with the infected person and their belongings.
  • Vector-borne diseases (malaria, filariasis, dengue, chikungunya): control or eliminate vectors and their breeding places by avoiding stagnation of water, cleaning coolers regularly, using mosquito nets, introducing larvivorous fish such as Gambusia in ponds, spraying insecticides in ditches, drainage areas and swamps, and fitting doors and windows with wire mesh.
  • Vaccination and immunisation programmes against diseases such as polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus; antibiotics and other drugs for treatment.
  • Education and awareness about diseases and their modes of transmission.

ncert_questions.q: In which way has the study of biology helped us to control infectious diseases?
ncert_questions.a:
The study of biology has helped in the following ways:

  • It identified the pathogens responsible for each disease (for example Salmonella typhi for typhoid, Plasmodium for malaria) and their life cycles and modes of transmission, so that the chain of spread can be broken (vector control for malaria, clean water for typhoid).
  • It gave us an understanding of the immune system, which led to vaccines and immunisation programmes; smallpox has been eradicated and polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus are largely controlled.
  • Biotechnology is at the verge of making newer and safer vaccines, such as the hepatitis B vaccine produced in yeast.
  • The discovery of antibiotics and other drugs has made it possible to treat infectious diseases effectively.
  • Diagnostic tests such as the Widal test (typhoid) and ELISA (HIV) allow early detection.

ncert_questions.q: How does the transmission of each of the following diseases take place? (a) Amoebiasis (b) Malaria (c) Ascariasis (d) Pneumonia
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Amoebiasis: caused by Entamoeba histolytica. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers and transfer the parasite from the faeces of an infected person to food and food products, contaminating them. Drinking water and food contaminated by faecal matter are the main sources of infection.

(b) Malaria: caused by Plasmodium. Transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, which injects sporozoites into the blood of a healthy person. The mosquito acquires the parasite (gametocytes) when it bites an infected person.

(c) Ascariasis: caused by the roundworm Ascaris. Eggs of the parasite are excreted with the faeces of infected persons and contaminate soil, water and plants. A healthy person acquires the infection through contaminated vegetables, fruits and water.

(d) Pneumonia: caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. A healthy person acquires the infection by inhaling droplets or aerosols released by an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils with an infected person.

ncert_questions.q: What measures would you take to prevent water-borne diseases?
ncert_questions.a:
Water-borne diseases such as typhoid, amoebiasis, ascariasis and cholera can be prevented by:

  • Drinking only clean water: boiled, filtered or properly treated water; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, tanks and cesspools.
  • Washing vegetables and fruits thoroughly and eating properly cooked food; standard hygiene practices in public catering.
  • Proper disposal of waste and excreta so that water sources are not contaminated by faecal matter; keeping sewage away from drinking water lines.
  • Personal hygiene: washing hands before eating and after using the toilet.
  • Controlling houseflies, which act as mechanical carriers of Entamoeba histolytica, and keeping food covered.
  • Vaccination where available (for example against typhoid) and public education.

ncert_questions.q: Discuss with your teacher what does a 'suitable gene' mean, in the context of DNA vaccines.
ncert_questions.a: A DNA vaccine works by introducing into the body a piece of pathogen DNA that codes for an antigenic protein of that pathogen. A 'suitable' gene is exactly this segment: it must code for a protein that sits on the pathogen's surface and is recognised by the host's immune system, so that once the gene is taken up and expressed inside host cells, the antigen it produces triggers antibody formation and the generation of memory B and T cells, without any live or even inactivated pathogen ever entering the body. Choosing a gene that does not correspond to such an antigenic protein would not train the immune system, so the choice of gene is what makes the vaccine work.

ncert_questions.q: Name the primary and secondary lymphoid organs.
ncert_questions.a:
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus. Here immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes (B cells in the bone marrow, T cells in the thymus).

Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and appendix. Here mature lymphocytes interact with antigens and proliferate to become effector cells.

ncert_questions.q: The following are some well-known abbreviations which have been used in this chapter. Expand each one to its full form: (a) MALT (b) CMI (c) AIDS (d) NACO (e) HIV
ncert_questions.a:
(a) MALT: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue.
(b) CMI: Cell-Mediated Immunity.
(c) AIDS: Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome.
(d) NACO: National AIDS Control Organisation.
(e) HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate the following and give examples of each: (a) Innate and acquired immunity (b) Active and passive immunity
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Innate versus acquired immunity.

  • Innate immunity is non-specific; acquired immunity is pathogen-specific.
  • Innate immunity is present at birth; acquired immunity is acquired after exposure to a pathogen during life.
  • Innate immunity has no memory; acquired immunity is characterised by memory (a stronger secondary response).
  • Innate immunity consists of barriers: physical (skin, mucus), physiological (stomach acid, saliva, tears), cellular (neutrophils, monocytes, NK cells, macrophages) and cytokine (interferons). Acquired immunity is carried out by B-lymphocytes (antibodies, humoral response) and T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated response).

(b) Active versus passive immunity.

  • In active immunity the host's own body produces antibodies on exposure to antigens; in passive immunity ready-made antibodies are given directly.
  • Active immunity is slow to develop but long-lasting (memory cells form); passive immunity is immediate but short-lived (no memory).
  • Examples of active immunity: natural infection, vaccination. Examples of passive immunity: IgA antibodies in colostrum given to the infant, antibodies passed from mother to foetus through the placenta, injection of antitoxin for tetanus or of antibodies against snake venom.

ncert_questions.q: Draw a well-labelled diagram of an antibody molecule.
ncert_questions.a: Draw a Y-shaped molecule made of four polypeptide chains: two long heavy chains forming the stem and the inner part of the arms, and two short light chains lying along the outer side of each arm. Show disulphide bonds linking the light chain to the heavy chain in each arm and linking the two heavy chains in the stem. Label the tip of each arm as the antigen-binding site. Write the formula H2L2. Labels expected by the marking scheme: heavy chain, light chain, antigen-binding site, disulphide bond (and, optionally, variable region and constant region).

ncert_questions.q: What are the various routes by which transmission of human immunodeficiency virus takes place?
ncert_questions.a:
HIV is transmitted through body fluids by:

  1. Sexual contact with an infected person.
  2. Transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products.
  3. Sharing infected needles and syringes, as by intravenous drug abusers.
  4. From an infected mother to her child through the placenta.

HIV does not spread by mere touch or physical contact. People at high risk are those with multiple sexual partners, intravenous drug addicts, people needing repeated blood transfusions and children born to HIV-infected mothers.

ncert_questions.q: What is the mechanism by which the AIDS virus causes deficiency of the immune system of the infected person?
ncert_questions.a: After entering the body, HIV enters macrophages. Its RNA genome is copied into viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. The viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cell to produce virus particles; the macrophages keep producing virus and act like an HIV factory. Simultaneously HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses, which are released into the blood and attack other helper T cells. This is repeated, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes. Since helper T cells are needed to activate B cells and other T cells, the person becomes unable to mount an immune response and suffers from bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss, and from infections by bacteria such as Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma.

ncert_questions.q: How is a cancerous cell different from a normal cell?
ncert_questions.a:
• Normal cells show contact inhibition: contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells have lost contact inhibition and continue to divide, forming a mass of cells called a tumour.
  • Normal cells divide in a regulated way and differentiate; cancer (neoplastic) cells divide rapidly and uncontrollably and are poorly differentiated.
  • Normal cells stay in their tissue; malignant cancer cells invade and damage surrounding tissue, compete with normal cells for vital nutrients, and can be sloughed off into the blood to start new tumours at distant sites (metastasis).
  • Normal cells have a limited number of divisions and undergo programmed death; cancer cells appear immortal in culture.

ncert_questions.q: Explain what is meant by metastasis.
ncert_questions.a: Metastasis is the property of malignant tumours by which cells sloughed off from the tumour reach distant sites through the blood, and wherever they get lodged in the body they start a new tumour. It is the most feared property of malignant tumours because the cancer spreads from its site of origin to other organs. Benign tumours do not show metastasis; they remain confined to their original location.

ncert_questions.q: List the harmful effects caused by alcohol/drug abuse.
ncert_questions.a:
• Immediate effects: reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence.
  • Overdose: excessive doses lead to coma and death due to respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage; combining drugs, or taking them with alcohol, often causes overdosing.
  • Warning signs in youth: drop in academic performance, absence from school, lack of interest in personal hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, fatigue, aggressive and rebellious behaviour, deteriorating relationships, loss of interest in hobbies, changed sleeping and eating habits, fluctuating weight and appetite.
  • Social and family effects: stealing to obtain money for drugs; mental and financial distress to the family and society.
  • Infections: intravenous drug abusers who share needles risk AIDS and hepatitis B.
  • Organ damage: chronic use damages the nervous system and the liver (cirrhosis); use during pregnancy adversely affects the foetus.
  • Drugs in sports: anabolic steroids cause masculinisation, abnormal menstrual cycles and deepening of voice in females; reduced testicle size, decreased sperm production, breast enlargement and baldness in males; and premature closure of growth centres of long bones with stunted growth in the young.

ncert_questions.q: Do you think that friends can influence one to take alcohol/drugs? If yes, how may one protect himself/herself from such an influence?
ncert_questions.a:
Yes. Peer pressure is one of the main reasons adolescents first try alcohol, tobacco or drugs; the wish to be accepted, curiosity, the need for adventure and the belief that it is 'cool' are all reinforced by friends. One can protect oneself by:

  • Learning to say no and avoiding undue peer pressure; choosing friends who do not abuse drugs.
  • Education and counselling about the effects of drugs, so that decisions are informed and stress is handled by healthy outlets such as sports, reading, music and yoga.
  • Seeking help from parents and teachers immediately when pressured, instead of hiding the problem.
  • Being alert to the danger signs in oneself and friends, and taking professional or medical help (psychologists, psychiatrists, de-addiction centres) when needed.

ncert_questions.q: Why is it that once a person starts taking alcohol or drugs, it is difficult to get rid of this habit?
ncert_questions.a: Because of addiction and dependence. Addiction is a psychological attachment to the euphoria and temporary feeling of well-being the drug produces, which drives the person to take it even when it is not needed. With repeated use the tolerance of the receptors in the body increases, so the receptors respond only to higher doses, leading to greater intake. Dependence means that if regular intake is stopped abruptly the body shows an unpleasant withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating), which in severe cases can be life-threatening. To avoid these symptoms the person keeps taking the drug, and dependence leads him or her to ignore social norms to obtain it. The habit is therefore very hard to give up without professional help.

ncert_questions.q: In your view what motivates youngsters to take to alcohol or drugs and how can this be avoided?
ncert_questions.a:
Motivations: curiosity, the need for adventure and excitement, and experimentation; pressure from peers; the wish to excel in school or examinations and escape from stress; unstable or unsupportive family structures; and television, movies, newspapers and the internet that project smoking and drinking as fashionable. Adolescence (12 to 18 years) is a vulnerable phase in which these pressures act strongly.

How to avoid it: avoid undue peer pressure and do not push a child to perform beyond their threshold; education and counselling to face problems and to accept disappointments and failures as part of life, channelising energy into sports, reading, music and yoga; seeking help from parents and peers; looking for danger signs so that parents and teachers can act early; and seeking professional and medical help from psychologists, psychiatrists and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes.

pyq.answer: c

pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Thymus and bone marrow are primary lymphoid organs where lymphocytes mature; the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and appendix are secondary.

pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT names Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton as the ringworm fungi. Aspergillus is not one of them.
