pyq.q: Assertion (A): The secondary immune response to a pathogen is faster and stronger than the primary response. Reason (R): The first encounter leaves memory B and T cells that recognise the pathogen on re-exposure.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The anamnestic response is due to the memory of the first encounter carried in memory cells, so R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A malaria patient experiences chills and high fever every three to four days. Reason (R): Sporozoites released from the liver directly cause the fever.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The fever is caused by haemozoin, the toxic substance released when infected RBCs rupture, not by sporozoites; so A is true and R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Vaccination provides active immunity. Reason (R): A vaccine contains antigenic proteins or a weakened pathogen that makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because the body makes its own antibodies and memory B and T cells in response to the vaccine, vaccination is active immunisation; R is the reason.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Benign tumours spread to distant organs through the blood. Reason (R): Cells sloughed off from a malignant tumour reach distant sites through the blood and start new tumours there.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Benign tumours remain confined to their original location and do not spread, so A is false. R correctly describes metastasis, a property of malignant tumours, so R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Intravenous drug abusers who share needles are at high risk of AIDS and hepatitis B. Reason (R): The viruses of both diseases are transmitted through infected needles and syringes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both HIV and hepatitis B virus are blood-borne and pass through contaminated needles, which is exactly why needle sharing is a high-risk practice.

pyq.q: State the functions of mast cells in an allergic response.
pyq.answer: Mast cells carry IgE antibodies on their surface. When an allergen (dust mite, pollen, animal dander) binds to these IgE molecules, the mast cells release chemicals like histamine and serotonin. These chemicals cause the symptoms of allergy: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing.
pyq.solution: Two marking points: IgE on mast cells; release of histamine and serotonin producing the symptoms.

pyq.q: Name the type of immune response the body produces on a second encounter with the same pathogen. Why is it more intense than the first response?
pyq.answer: The response is the secondary or anamnestic response. It is highly intensified because the immune system carries a memory of the first encounter: memory B and T cells formed during the primary response recognise the pathogen quickly and produce antibodies in large amounts within a short time.
pyq.solution: Name (anamnestic) + reason (memory cells).

pyq.q: Name the toxic substance released by the malarial parasite in the human body. Why does the patient feel chills and a high fever?
pyq.answer: The toxic substance is haemozoin. It is released when the Plasmodium parasites multiplying inside the red blood cells rupture the RBCs. Haemozoin is responsible for the chill and high fever, which recur every three to four days as fresh batches of RBCs rupture.
pyq.solution: Haemozoin; released on RBC rupture; recurring every 3–4 days.

pyq.q: Why are breast-fed babies more immune to diseases than bottle-fed babies?
pyq.answer: The mother's milk, especially the colostrum secreted during the first days of lactation, contains abundant antibodies of the IgA class. These ready-made antibodies give the breast-fed infant passive immunity against many infections. Bottle-fed babies do not receive these antibodies and are therefore less protected.
pyq.solution: Colostrum, IgA, passive immunity.

pyq.q: Mention two roles of the spleen in the human body.
pyq.answer: The spleen is a large bean-shaped secondary lymphoid organ. (i) It acts as a filter of the blood, trapping blood-borne micro-organisms with its lymphocytes and phagocytes and mounting an immune response. (ii) It has a large reservoir of erythrocytes.
pyq.solution: Filter of blood; reservoir of RBCs.

pyq.q: Distinguish between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour.
pyq.answer:
Benign tumour: remains confined to its original location, does not spread to other parts of the body and causes little damage.
Malignant tumour: a mass of proliferating neoplastic cells that grows rapidly, invades and damages the surrounding normal tissues, competes with normal cells for nutrients, and spreads to distant sites through the blood to start new tumours (metastasis).
pyq.solution: Confined versus invasive with metastasis.

pyq.q: What are 'withdrawal symptoms'? Name any two.
pyq.answer: Withdrawal symptoms are the characteristic and unpleasant symptoms the body shows when regular intake of a drug or alcohol on which it has become dependent is abruptly discontinued. Examples: anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating. In severe cases they may be life-threatening, which is why de-addiction needs medical supervision.
pyq.solution: Definition tied to dependence; any two of anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating.

pyq.q: Name the four types of barriers that constitute innate immunity. Give one example of each.
pyq.answer:
1. Physical barriers: the skin, which prevents entry of micro-organisms; the mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts, which traps microbes.
  2. Physiological barriers: acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes, which prevent microbial growth.
  3. Cellular barriers: leukocytes such as polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes and natural killer lymphocytes in the blood, and macrophages in tissues, which phagocytose and destroy microbes.
  4. Cytokine barriers: interferons, secreted by virus-infected cells, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

All four are non-specific and present from birth.
pyq.solution: Four barriers, each with an example, 0.5 + 0.25 pattern in most schemes.

pyq.q: Explain how the DNA of a retrovirus gets incorporated into the host cell's genome and what follows in the case of HIV.
pyq.answer: HIV is a retrovirus with an RNA genome inside an envelope. After entering a host cell (first a macrophage), the viral RNA is copied into viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA in the nucleus. The integrated viral DNA then directs the infected cell to produce virus particles: it is transcribed into viral RNA and viral proteins, new viruses are assembled and released. Macrophages keep producing virus and act as an HIV factory. The virus then infects helper T-lymphocytes, replicates in them and progressively reduces their number, so the person cannot mount an immune response and suffers from opportunistic infections; this is AIDS.
pyq.solution: Reverse transcriptase; integration; production of virus; helper T cell decline.

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of an antibody molecule and mention the four classes of antibodies named in NCERT.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: a Y-shaped molecule with two long heavy chains forming the stem and inner arms and two short light chains along the outer arms, joined by disulphide bonds; the tips of the arms are the antigen-binding sites. Formula H2L2.

Classes: IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG. Antibodies are produced by B-lymphocytes, and because they are found in the blood the response they mediate is called the humoral immune response.
pyq.solution: Diagram with four labels (2 marks) + classes (1 mark).

pyq.q: What is cancer? How is it detected and treated?
pyq.answer:
Cancer is the uncontrolled proliferation of cells that have lost contact inhibition, forming masses called tumours; malignant tumours invade surrounding tissue and spread by metastasis.

Detection: biopsy and histopathological study of the tissue; blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in leukaemia; radiography (X-rays), CT scan and MRI for cancers of internal organs; antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular biology techniques to detect genes conferring inherited susceptibility.

Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy (lethal irradiation of tumour cells while protecting normal tissue), chemotherapy (drugs with side effects such as hair loss and anaemia), usually in combination; and immunotherapy with biological response modifiers such as α-interferon, which activate the patient's immune system to destroy the tumour.
pyq.solution: Definition 1, detection 1, treatment 1.

pyq.q: Why should needles and syringes not be shared? Name two diseases that spread this way and state how each can be prevented.
pyq.answer:
Infected needles and syringes carry blood containing viruses, so sharing them transfers the infection directly into the bloodstream of the next user. Two diseases spread this way are AIDS (caused by HIV) and hepatitis B (a liver infection). Intravenous drug abusers who share needles are at the highest risk.

Prevention: use of disposable needles and syringes in hospitals and by any injecting user; screening blood in blood banks so that transfusions are safe; controlling drug abuse; and, for hepatitis B, vaccination with the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine produced in yeast. For AIDS there is no vaccine, so education (NACO), safe sex and regular check-ups are advocated.
pyq.solution: Reason, two diseases, prevention of each.

pyq.q: State the side effects of anabolic steroids abused by sportspersons in (a) females and (b) males.
pyq.answer:
(a) In females: masculinisation (features like males), increased aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles, excessive hair growth on the face and body, enlargement of the clitoris and deepening of the voice.

(b) In males: acne, increased aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, reduction in the size of the testicles, decreased sperm production, potential for kidney and liver dysfunction, breast enlargement, premature baldness and enlargement of the prostate gland.

In adolescents of both sexes there is severe facial and body acne and premature closure of the growth centres of the long bones, leading to stunted growth.
pyq.solution: Three effects for each sex, plus the growth effect, is a full-mark answer.

pyq.q: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium in the human host and in the mosquito with the help of a labelled diagram. Why is the mosquito called the vector?
pyq.answer:
In the human host: An infected female Anopheles injects sporozoites (the infective stage) into the blood while biting. The sporozoites reach the liver, where they multiply asexually in the liver cells. The parasites then burst out and enter the red blood cells, multiply further and rupture the RBCs, releasing the toxic substance haemozoin, which causes the characteristic chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. Some parasites inside the RBCs develop into the sexual stages, male and female gametocytes.

In the mosquito: When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, the gametocytes enter her body with the blood. Fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's gut, producing sporozoites that migrate to and are stored in the salivary glands. When this mosquito bites a healthy person the sporozoites are injected, and the cycle continues.

Thus Plasmodium requires two hosts: the human, in which asexual multiplication occurs, and the female Anopheles, in which sexual reproduction occurs. The mosquito is called the vector because it carries the parasite from an infected person to a healthy person and transmits the disease.

Diagram: draw the cycle as in NCERT Fig 7.1 with labels: mosquito injects sporozoites; sporozoites enter liver and multiply; parasites enter RBCs; RBC rupture releases haemozoin (fever); gametocytes formed; mosquito takes up gametocytes; fertilisation in gut; sporozoites in salivary glands.
pyq.solution: Human phase 2, mosquito phase 1.5, diagram 1, vector 0.5 is a typical split.

pyq.q: What is AIDS? Explain how HIV replicates in the human body and leads to immune deficiency. Mention two ways by which its spread can be prevented.
pyq.answer:
AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is a deficiency of the immune system acquired during a person's lifetime, caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), a retrovirus with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome. It is transmitted by sexual contact, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing infected needles and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta; not by touch.

Replication and immune deficiency: After entry the virus infects macrophages. Its RNA is copied into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase; the viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the cell to make virus particles, so the macrophages act as an HIV factory. The virus also enters helper T-lymphocytes, replicates there and releases progeny viruses that infect more helper T cells. Repeated cycles cause a progressive decrease in helper T cells. Since helper T cells are needed to activate B cells and other T cells, the person can no longer produce an effective immune response, suffers bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss, and falls prey to infections by Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites such as Toxoplasma. Diagnosis is by ELISA; anti-retroviral drugs are only partially effective. The time-lag between infection and symptoms is 5 to 10 years.

Prevention (any two): ensuring blood from blood banks is safe; using disposable needles and syringes; free distribution of condoms and advocating safe sex; controlling drug abuse; regular HIV check-ups in susceptible populations; education through NACO and NGOs.
pyq.solution: Definition and cause 1, replication mechanism 2.5, immune deficiency 0.5, prevention 1.

pyq.q: Explain the role of the primary and secondary lymphoid organs in the immune system. Describe the structure of an antibody and distinguish between humoral and cell-mediated immunity.
pyq.answer:
Primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) are where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes. The bone marrow produces all blood cells including lymphocytes and is where B cells mature; the thymus, a lobed organ near the heart beneath the breastbone, is where T cells mature. The thymus is large at birth and shrinks with age. Secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix) are the sites where the mature lymphocytes interact with antigens and proliferate to become effector cells. The spleen filters blood and stores erythrocytes; lymph nodes trap antigens in lymph and tissue fluid and activate lymphocytes. MALT in the mucosal linings makes up about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue.

Antibody structure: a Y-shaped protein of four peptide chains, two small light chains and two longer heavy chains (H2L2), held by disulphide bonds, with antigen-binding sites at the tips of the arms. Classes: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG.

Humoral immunity is mediated by B-lymphocytes, which secrete antibodies into the blood (body fluids) to act against pathogens present there. Cell-mediated immunity is mediated by T-lymphocytes, which do not secrete antibodies but attack infected or foreign cells directly and help B cells; it is responsible for the rejection of grafts, which is why tissue matching and immuno-suppressants are needed in transplantation.
pyq.solution: Lymphoid organs 2, antibody 1.5, humoral vs CMI 1.5.

pyq.q: What is drug addiction? Explain the terms tolerance and dependence. Discuss the measures suggested by NCERT for the prevention and control of drug and alcohol abuse among adolescents.
pyq.answer:
Addiction is a psychological attachment to certain effects of a drug or alcohol, such as euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being, which drives the person to take the substance even when it is not needed or when it harms health. Tolerance develops with repeated use: the tolerance level of the receptors in the body increases, so they respond only to higher doses, which leads to greater intake. Dependence is the tendency of the body to show a characteristic and unpleasant withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) if regular intake is abruptly stopped; in severe cases it may be life-threatening. Dependence makes the person ignore social norms to obtain the drug.

Prevention and control:

  1. Avoid undue peer pressure: every child has their own choice and personality and should not be pushed beyond their threshold in studies, sports or other activities.
  2. Education and counselling: help the young to face problems and stresses and to accept disappointments and failures as part of life; channel their energy into sports, reading, music, yoga and other healthy activities.
  3. Seeking help from parents and peers: immediate guidance from parents and trusted friends when a problem arises.
  4. Looking for danger signs: alert parents and teachers should notice signs such as falling grades, absence, isolation, changed habits, and intervene.
  5. Seeking professional and medical help: psychologists, psychiatrists and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes can help the affected person overcome the problem completely and lead a normal life.
pyq.solution: Addiction 1, tolerance 0.5, dependence 1, five measures 2.5.

pyq.q:
A 24-year-old man returned from a rural area and developed bouts of chills followed by high fever that recurred every third day. A blood smear showed a protozoan parasite inside his red blood cells. He was treated and recovered.
(i) Name the disease and the causative organism, and mention which species causes its most serious form.
(ii) Why did the fever recur in cycles?
(iii) Name the vector and the stage of the parasite it injects.
(iv) Suggest two measures the village could adopt to stop further cases.
pyq.answer:
(i) Malaria, caused by the protozoan Plasmodium; Plasmodium falciparum causes the most serious, malignant malaria.

(ii) The parasites multiply inside red blood cells and rupture them in batches; each rupture releases the toxic substance haemozoin, which causes the chill and high fever every three to four days.

(iii) The female Anopheles mosquito; it injects sporozoites.

(iv) Any two: prevent stagnation of water and clean coolers regularly; use mosquito nets and wire mesh on doors and windows; introduce Gambusia fish into ponds to eat larvae; spray insecticides in ditches, drainage areas and swamps.
pyq.solution: One mark per sub-question.

pyq.q:
The graph below (described) shows antibody concentration against time. A first injection of antigen X produced a small rise in antibody after a lag of about a week, which then declined. A second injection of X four weeks later produced a much larger and faster rise that persisted for weeks. When antigen Y was injected together with the second dose of X, the response to Y was small and slow.
(i) Name the responses to the first and second injections of X.
(ii) Why is the response to the second injection of X greater?
(iii) Why was the response to Y small even though it was given at the same time as the second dose of X?
(iv) Which principle of immunisation does this experiment illustrate?
pyq.answer:
(i) First injection: primary immune response; second injection: secondary or anamnestic immune response.

(ii) During the primary response memory B and T cells specific to X were formed; on re-exposure they recognise X immediately and produce antibodies rapidly and in much larger amounts.

(iii) Acquired immunity is pathogen (antigen) specific. The memory cells formed were for X, not Y, so the body met Y for the first time and produced only a primary response to it.

(iv) The principle of memory of the immune system, on which vaccination is based: a vaccine (antigenic proteins or weakened pathogen) generates memory cells so that a real infection later meets a fast, strong secondary response.
pyq.solution: One mark per sub-question; specificity and memory are the two ideas tested.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer. A hospital laboratory receives a blood sample from a patient with repeated fevers, persistent diarrhoea and weight loss over several months. The ELISA test is positive. The patient's history shows that he received blood transfusions after an accident eight years ago.
(i) Name the disease indicated and its causative agent, and expand ELISA.
(ii) Which cells of the immune system are progressively lost in this disease, and why does that make the patient prone to infections?
(iii) How might the patient have contracted the infection, and why did symptoms appear only now?
(iv) State two precautions hospitals should take to prevent such transmission.
pyq.answer:
(i) AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome), caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), a retrovirus. ELISA: enzyme-linked immuno-sorbent assay.

(ii) Helper T-lymphocytes. HIV replicates in them and releases progeny that infect more helper T cells, steadily reducing their number. Helper T cells are needed to activate B cells and other T cells, so without them the body cannot mount an immune response and is infected by bacteria such as Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma.

(iii) Through transfusion of contaminated blood. There is a time-lag between infection and the appearance of AIDS symptoms, which may be 5 to 10 years, during which the virus multiplies in macrophages and helper T cells.

(iv) Screen all blood in blood banks to ensure it is free of HIV; use disposable needles and syringes; and advise regular HIV check-ups for people who need repeated transfusions.
pyq.solution: One mark per part; naming helper T cells and ELISA's full form are the common misses.

practice_mcq.explanation: Preformed antibodies are given directly for a quick response, so it is passive immunisation.

practice_mcq.q: The organism used to produce the hepatitis B vaccine by recombinant DNA technology is
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT names the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast.

practice_mcq.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is an example of
practice_mcq.explanation: The body attacks its own joint tissues; it is NCERT's example of auto-immunity.

practice_mcq.q: Which lymphoid organ is quite large at birth and keeps reducing in size with age?
practice_mcq.explanation: The thymus is large at birth and very small by puberty.

practice_mcq.q: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) constitutes about what fraction of the lymphoid tissue in the human body?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives MALT as about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue.

practice_mcq.q: HIV first enters and multiplies in
practice_mcq.explanation: Macrophages are the first target and act as an HIV factory; helper T cells are attacked next.

practice_mcq.q: The enzyme that copies the RNA of HIV into DNA is
practice_mcq.explanation: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase to make viral DNA from their RNA genome.

practice_mcq.q: Cells which show contact inhibition are
practice_mcq.explanation: Normal cells stop growing on contact with other cells; cancer cells have lost this property.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a non-ionising carcinogenic radiation?
practice_mcq.explanation: UV is non-ionising; X-rays and gamma rays are ionising. All three damage DNA.

practice_mcq.q: The biological response modifier used in immunotherapy of cancer is
practice_mcq.explanation: α-interferon activates the patient's immune system against the tumour.

practice_mcq.explanation: Morphine from the opium poppy is acetylated to heroin. Cannabis gives cannabinoids and Erythroxylum gives cocaine.

practice_mcq.q: Marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja are all obtained from
practice_mcq.explanation: The flower tops, leaves and resin of Cannabis sativa produce these cannabinoid preparations.

practice_mcq.explanation: Adrenaline and nor-adrenaline raise blood pressure and heart rate, which is why smoking strains the heart.

practice_mcq.explanation: This is NCERT's listed effect of anabolic steroids in adolescent boys and girls.

common_mistakes: Writing 'absence of disease' as the definition of health. The examiner expects 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being'.

Confusing the stages of Plasmodium: the mosquito injects sporozoites and picks up gametocytes. Writing the reverse loses the whole life-cycle mark, and forgetting haemozoin loses the fever explanation.
Mixing the diagnostic tests: Widal test is for typhoid, ELISA for HIV, biopsy with histopathology for cancer. A wrong test in a 1-mark question scores zero.
Putting the skin under physiological barriers or stomach acid under physical barriers. Learn the four innate barriers with their exact NCERT examples.
Calling vaccination passive immunity because 'something is injected'. Vaccination is active; injecting an antitoxin or preformed antibodies is passive.
Writing IgG instead of IgE for allergy, or IgG instead of IgA for colostrum. The antibody class is usually the second mark of the question.
Saying HIV attacks B cells or red blood cells. HIV multiplies first in macrophages and then destroys helper T-lymphocytes; the order matters in the marking scheme.
Attributing metastasis to benign tumours, or describing malignant tumours without the words 'invade', 'sloughed off', 'blood' and 'new tumour at a distant site'.
Reversing heroin and cocaine: heroin is a depressant that slows body functions, cocaine is a CNS stimulant that interferes with dopamine transport.

Giving generic answers to 'harmful effects of drug abuse' or 'prevention measures' instead of NCERT's specific points (reckless behaviour, overdose deaths, needle-borne AIDS and hepatitis B; peer pressure, counselling, danger signs, professional help).
Spelling and italics: Salmonella typhi, Entamoeba histolytica, Wuchereria bancrofti, Papaver somniferum, Erythroxylum coca. Genus capitalised, species in lower case, both underlined when handwritten.
strategy:
This chapter is memory-heavy, so plan around three passes. In the first pass, build the disease table for the eight diseases of section 7.1: pathogen, organ, two symptoms, mode of transmission. Say the eight rows aloud until you can reproduce them in under three minutes; they feed every 1-mark and 'complete the table' question. In the same pass learn the malaria life cycle with the diagram, drawing it twice from memory with all labels.

In the second pass, do immunity as a set of contrasts: innate versus acquired, humoral versus cell-mediated, active versus passive, primary versus secondary response, primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, allergy versus auto-immunity. Write each contrast as three lines with one example. Draw the antibody molecule and the types-of-immunity flow chart. Fix the four innate barriers with their examples.

In the third pass, take AIDS, cancer and drug abuse as three 5-mark answers: HIV replication (macrophage factory, then helper T cells, reverse transcriptase, ELISA, prevention), cancer (contact inhibition, benign versus malignant, metastasis, carcinogens, detection, treatment), and drugs (source plants, receptor or neurotransmitter, addiction, dependence, withdrawal, effects, five prevention measures). Write each one out once under timed conditions.

Time allocation in the paper: 1-mark items should take under a minute each; give a 3-mark answer five to six minutes with a point-wise layout; give a 5-mark answer ten minutes and always include the diagram where one exists. Use NCERT's exact terms (haemozoin, anamnestic, contact inhibition, neoplastic, diacetylmorphine); the marking scheme is built on them.
